summary: Specifies the Simple Mail Transfer Protocol, the way hosts transfer electronic mail to each other. It was based on the earlier Mail Transfer Protocol work. Replaced by RFC 821.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 788 specifies how one host transfers mail to another through a sequence of commands and replies. A transaction identifies the sender, lists recipients, and sends the message data; a host can relay mail to another host when needed. RFC 821 later replaced this specification.

questions: how does an smtp mail transaction work
subtitle: A command-and-reply protocol for transferring mail between hosts.

tldr.problem: Hosts need a common procedure for transferring mail reliably, including when sender and recipient hosts use different transport environments.
tldr.mechanism: SMTP uses a lock-step exchange of commands and replies to identify the sender, name recipients, and transfer message data; relay hosts can forward mail onward.

facts.label: Message end marker
facts.value: A line containing only a period

sections.title: The SMTP Conversation
sections.content:
The sender SMTP establishes a full-duplex channel to a receiver SMTP, which may be the final destination or an intermediate host. The sender sends commands and the receiver replies to them. The exchange proceeds one step at a time.

Mail can go directly between hosts that share a transport service or pass through one or more relay servers. The sender uses a reverse-path to identify where error reports should go and a forward-path to identify the next destination.
sections.plainLanguage: One mail server opens a connection and gives commands; the other answers each one. If the recipient is elsewhere, an intermediate server can pass the message onward.

sections.title: A Mail Transaction
sections.content:
A basic transaction starts with MAIL, which gives the sender's reverse-path. One or more RCPT commands give recipient forward-paths. The receiver can accept or reject each recipient separately. Then DATA starts the message text, which ends with a line containing only a period. The receiver processes the transaction and replies.

The reverse-path can be used for error reports. A forward-path can include relay hosts. As a message is relayed, each relay moves its own identifier from the forward-path to the reverse-path. If delivery later fails, the relay sends an undeliverable-mail notice toward the originator.
sections.plainLanguage: The sender identifies itself, names one or more recipients, and sends the message. The receiver can reject a recipient without rejecting every other recipient in the transaction.

sections.title: Commands, Replies, and Data
sections.content:
Commands are character strings terminated by CRLF. The RFC defines commands for starting mail, naming recipients, sending data, opening and closing a connection, and optional tasks such as verifying a user or expanding a list. Commands and replies are not case-sensitive, but mailbox user names may be case-sensitive.

Replies include a numeric code and text. During DATA, a line containing only a period ends the message data; the transparency procedure prevents a period at the start of message text from being mistaken for that marker. The RFC also describes optional commands for sending a message to a user's terminal as well as, or instead of, a mailbox.
sections.plainLanguage: SMTP commands have a defined order, and reply codes report what happened. A line containing only a period marks the end of the message data.
